entry: American [[Country music|country]] singer and songwriter. His style blends traditional country with pop and rock, and he is the only artist to have released nine albums certified Diamond by the Recording Industry Association of America, surpassing [[The Beatles]]' former record of six. He has sold more than 170 million records and, according to the RIAA, is the best-selling solo albums artist in the United States, with 162 million domestic units. Brooks retired from recording from 2001 to 2005 and later performed in a [[Las Vegas]] concert residency. In 2020 he became the youngest recipient of the [[Library of Congress]] Gershwin Prize for Popular Song.

Eagle-like deity in Hindu mythology, the mount (vahana) of [[Vishnu]]. Described as king of the birds and an enemy of every serpent, Garuda is mentioned in the Hindu, Buddhist and Jain faiths and in the [[Vedas]]. He is the son of the sage Kashyapa and Vinata and the younger brother of Aruna, charioteer of the [[Sun]]. Garuda is part of the state insignia of [[India]], [[Indonesia]] and [[Thailand]], and is the coat of arms of Indonesia and Thailand.

American actor and child star, known for playing Arnold Jackson in the [[Sitcom|sitcom]] *Diff'rent Strokes* (1978–1986). He was the highest-paid child actor on television in the late 1970s and 1980s. Medications for a [[Kidney|kidney]] disease, including corticosteroids, limited his growth to 4 ft 8 in (142 cm). In 1989 he sued his parents and business adviser over the misuse of his assets, and about a decade later he declared [[Bankruptcy]]. His later career consisted largely of guest appearances, often playing himself. He died of an epidural hematoma caused by a fall at his home in Santaquin, Utah.

American film actor known for his strong, silent screen persona and understated style. Born in Helena, [[Montana]], he began as a film extra and stunt rider before establishing himself in [[Western (genre)|Western]] roles in [[Silent film|silent films]]. His first sound picture, *The Virginian* (1929), made him a movie star. He won [[Academy Awards]] for Best Actor for *Sergeant York* (1941) and *High Noon* (1952). His career spanned 36 years and included leading roles in 84 feature films, and he embodied the ideal American hero on screen. He received an honorary Academy Award in 1961, shortly before his death from prostate cancer.

English former footballer and sports broadcaster. He is the only player to have been the top goalscorer in England with three clubs, [[Leicester|Leicester City]], Everton and Tottenham Hotspur. He scored 48 goals in 80 caps for England, and his six goals at the 1986 [[FIFA World Cup]] won the Golden Boot. In a senior career of 16 years and 654 games, he scored 331 goals and never received a yellow or red card. He later presented the [[BBC]]'s flagship *Match of the Day* from 1999 until 2025, the longest tenure of any presenter. In 2018 he cofounded Goalhanger, a company that produces [[Podcast|podcasts]].

English actor and filmmaker. He won an Academy Award for playing [[Winston Churchill]] in *Darkest Hour* (2017), and his films have grossed over US$11 billion worldwide. He rose to prominence in British film as Sid Vicious in *Sid and Nancy* (1986) and later played [[Lee Harvey Oswald]] in *JFK* (1991) and [[Count Dracula]] in *Bram Stoker's Dracula* (1992). He played Sirius Black in the [[Harry Potter (film series)|Harry Potter]] films and James Gordon in *The Dark Knight* trilogy. He has also acted in music videos for [[David Bowie]] and Guns N' Roses, and was made a Knight Bachelor by [[Charles III]].

American [[Serial killer|serial killer]] known as the Green River Killer. He was convicted of murdering 49 women between 1982 and 1998 in the northwestern United States, most of them alleged prostitutes or other women in vulnerable circumstances. He had been a suspect since 1982, but investigators could not link him to the murders until advances in [[DNA profiling]] allowed them to do so. He was arrested in 2001 as he left a truck factory in Renton, [[Washington (state)|Washington]]. Under a plea bargain in which he agreed to disclose the locations of still-missing women, he was spared the death penalty and received life imprisonment without parole.

Giant planet composed mainly of hydrogen and helium. The [[Solar System]] has two gas giants, [[Jupiter]] and [[Saturn]]. The term was originally synonymous with giant planet, but from the 1970s [[Uranus]] and [[Neptune]] were increasingly classified separately as ice giants, which are composed mainly of heavier volatile substances. Jupiter and Saturn contain heavier elements making up between 3 and 13 percent of their mass. A layer of [[Metallic hydrogen|metallic hydrogen]] in the mid-interior would make up the bulk of the mass of every gas giant, because the very high pressure turns hydrogen into an electrical conductor. The boundary between gas giants and [[Brown dwarf|brown dwarfs]] is debated.

Continuous-flow [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engine]] in which compressed air is burned with fuel and the hot gas expands through a turbine. The turbine shaft drives the compressor and may also produce thrust, shaft power or both. Gas turbines with constant-pressure combustion operate on the Brayton cycle and power [[Aircraft|aircraft]], electric generators, ships and pumps. In aircraft the same core may drive turbojets, [[Turbofan|turbofans]], turboprops or turboshafts. A turbocharger contains a turbine but is not a gas-turbine engine, because it lacks a combustor. The first complete gas-turbine design was patented in 1791 by the Englishman John Barber. In 1903 the Norwegian Ægidius Elling built the first gas turbine to produce more power than it needed to run its own components. Sanford Alexander Moss, who joined [[General Electric]] that year, later applied gas-turbine concepts to the turbocharger.

Transparent, yellowish, flammable [[Petrochemical|petrochemical]] fuel for spark-ignited [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engines]]. Known as petrol in other English-speaking countries, it is made in [[Oil refinery|oil refineries]] by [[Distillation|distillation]] of petroleum and then blended with additives. The bulk of it is hydrocarbons with four to twelve carbon atoms per molecule. Roughly 72 liters (19 U.S. gal) of gasoline is derived from a 160-liter (42 U.S. gal) barrel of crude oil. Its [[Octane rating|octane rating]] measures resistance to premature ignition, or knocking. [[Tetraethyllead|Tetraethyl lead]] was once widely used to raise octane but is not used in modern automotive gasoline because of its health hazards. Gasoline may contain oxygen-containing chemicals such as [[Ethanol|ethanol]], MTBE or ETBE to improve combustion.

French mathematician, commonly presented as the inventor of descriptive geometry, the mathematical basis of [[Technical drawing|technical drawing]]. Born in Beaune, he studied at the Collège de la Trinité in [[Lyon]], where he became a teacher of physics at seventeen. He later worked as a draftsman at a military engineering school in Mézières, and is commonly called the father of [[Differential geometry|differential geometry]]. During the [[French Revolution]] he served as Minister of the Marine and helped found the École Polytechnique with Lazare Carnot and Lamblardie. With [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]] and others he contributed to the establishment of Arts et Métiers ParisTech. In 1798 he accompanied [[Napoleon]] to Egypt, where he helped found the Institut d'Égypte.

Branch of [[Medicine|medicine]] focused on the digestive system and its disorders. The digestive system moves material through the [[Gastrointestinal tract|gastrointestinal tract]] by peristalsis, digests it, absorbs nutrients and removes waste. Gastroenterologists treat conditions including gastroesophageal reflux disease, gastrointestinal bleeding, [[Irritable bowel syndrome]], inflammatory bowel disease such as [[Crohn's disease]] and ulcerative colitis, peptic ulcer disease, and colon polyps and cancer. [[Galen]]'s concept of the stomach having four faculties was widely accepted until the 17th century. In 1823 William Prout discovered that stomach juices contain [[Hydrochloric acid]]. In 2005 Barry Marshall and Robin Warren of Australia won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering [[Helicobacter pylori]].

Passageway of the digestive system that leads from the [[Mouth]] to the [[Anus]], also called the GI tract, digestive tract, gut or alimentary canal. In humans it consists of the [[Esophagus|esophagus]], [[Stomach|stomach]] and intestines, and is divided into upper and lower tracts. Food is digested to extract nutrients and energy, and waste is expelled at the anus as [[Feces|feces]]. The whole human tract is about nine meters (30 feet) long at autopsy but shorter in a living body, because the intestines maintain muscle tone. Most animals have a through-gut, though [[Sponge|sponges]] and [[Cnidaria|cnidarians]] have simpler arrangements. The human gut microbiota comprises around 4,000 different strains of bacteria, archaea, viruses and eukaryotes, and enteroendocrine cells release hormones that regulate digestion.

Class of [[Mollusca|molluscs]], including [[Snail|snails]] and slugs. With an estimated 65,000 to 80,000 living species, gastropods are the second-largest animal class after insects. Their fossil record extends back to the Late Cambrian. Gastropods live in marine, freshwater and terrestrial environments, from gardens and deserts to the deep sea and [[Hydrothermal vent|hydrothermal vents]]. Snails generally have a large external shell into which the body can retract, while slugs have no shell or a small internal one. Marine forms include [[Abalone|abalones]], conches, periwinkles and cowries. The name comes from Greek words meaning stomach and foot, a reference to the foot lying below the guts. [[Georges Cuvier]] described the group in 1795.

Rapid-firing multiple-barrel [[Firearm|firearm]], forerunner of the modern electric motor-driven rotary cannon. Richard Jordan Gatling, a [[North Carolina]] native, invented it in [[Indiana]] in 1861. Its barrels revolve around a central shaft as a hand crank turns, so that each barrel loads, fires and ejects in turn, which allowed high rates of fire without the barrels overheating. The Union Army used it in the [[American Civil War]], its first combat use. It was later used in the Boshin War, the Anglo-Zulu War and at San Juan Hill in the [[Spanish–American War]], and Pennsylvania militia used it in [[Pittsburgh]] during the Great Railroad Strike of 1877.

Early medieval [[Hinduism|Hindu]] philosopher and scholar of the [[Vedanta|Advaita Vedanta]] school. Details of his life are uncertain, and estimates place him between the 6th and 7th centuries. [[Adi Shankara]] called him the *paramaguru*, or highest teacher. He is credited as author or compiler of the *Māṇḍūkya Kārikā*, a verse explanation in four chapters of the Mandukya Upanishad. Its fourth chapter uses [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] terminology, but its doctrine is Vedantic rather than Buddhist. The first three chapters have been influential in Advaita Vedanta, and the text is considered the earliest extant systematic treatise on Advaita Vedanta, according to Sarma.

Bosonic elementary particle serving as the force carrier for [[Fermion|fermions]]. Photons, W and Z bosons, and gluons are gauge bosons, and all known ones have spin 1, making them vector bosons. The [[Higgs boson]], by comparison, has spin zero. In a quantized [[Gauge theory|gauge theory]], gauge bosons are quanta of the gauge fields. [[Quantum electrodynamics]] has one gauge boson, the photon, while [[Quantum chromodynamics|quantum chromodynamics]] has eight, the gluons. Isolated gluons do not occur because of color confinement. In the [[Standard Model]], the W and Z bosons gain mass through the Higgs mechanism, and the Higgs boson has been observed at the [[Large Hadron Collider]]. Gravity may be carried by the hypothetical [[Graviton]].

Physical [[Field (physics)|field theory]] whose Lagrangian is invariant under local transformations of a Lie group. Gauge fields are included to ensure this invariance, and their quanta are called [[Gauge boson|gauge bosons]]. The term gauge refers to a formalism that regulates redundant degrees of freedom in a physical system's Lagrangian. [[Quantum electrodynamics]] is an abelian gauge theory with symmetry group U(1), and the [[Standard Model]] is non-abelian with symmetry group U(1) × SU(2) × SU(3). Gauge theories also appear in [[General relativity|general relativity]]. [[Hermann Weyl]] introduced the name in 1918, in an attempt to generalize general relativity to include [[Electromagnetism|electromagnetism]]. Chen Ning Yang and Robert Mills generalized the concept to non-Abelian symmetries in 1954, in what is now called [[Yang–Mills theory]].

Historical region of [[Western Europe]] inhabited by Celtic tribes. It roughly covered present-day Belgium, France, Luxembourg, and parts of Germany, the Netherlands, northern [[Italy]] and Switzerland. Roman control lasted for five centuries, until the collapse of the [[Western Roman Empire]]. [[Julius Caesar]] subdued the largest part of Gaul in his campaigns from 58 to 51 BC. The Gauls shifted to a Gallo-Roman culture in [[Late antiquity|Late Antiquity]], and the name Gallia remained in use until the Capetian Kingdom of France emerged in the high medieval period. The Catholic Archbishop of Lyon still holds the title Primate of the Gauls.

Largest living [[Bovidae|bovid]], *Bos gaurus*, also called the Indian bison. It is native to the [[Indian subcontinent]] and [[Southeast Asia]] and is the largest of the wild cattle. Listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List since 1986, its global population was estimated at a maximum of 21,000 mature individuals in 2016, most of them in India. The gaur is massively built, with a high convex ridge on the forehead between the horns, a prominent back ridge, very large ears and a dewlap on the throat. Adult males are dark brown, and both sexes have horns. The domesticated gayal, or mithun, originated partly from the wild gaur and is most common in the border regions of Northeast India, Bangladesh and Myanmar.

[[Algorithm]] for solving systems of linear equations by row operations, named after [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]]. The three elementary row operations are swapping two rows, multiplying a row by a nonzero number, and adding a multiple of one row to another. These operations do not change the solution set. Forward elimination reduces the matrix to row echelon form, which shows whether a system has no solution, a unique solution or infinitely many, and back substitution then finds the solution. The method can also compute the rank of a [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]], its [[Determinant|determinant]] and the inverse of an invertible matrix. Reducing the matrix fully to reduced row echelon form is called Gauss–Jordan elimination. For an n × n system, the method has cubic time complexity, O(n³).

Bell-shaped [[Exponential function|exponential]] [[Function (mathematics)|function]] named after [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]]: f(x) = a·exp(−(x−b)²/2c²). The parameter a is the height of the peak, b its horizontal center, and c the width, which corresponds to the standard deviation. When normalized, a Gaussian is the probability density function of a [[Normal distribution|normal distribution]] with mean μ and variance σ². It is used in [[Signal processing|signal processing]] for Gaussian filters, in image processing for Gaussian blurs, and in solving heat and diffusion equations. Its indefinite integral is the [[Error function|error function]].

Province of [[South Africa]], the smallest by land area and the most populous, with 26% of the national population (pop., 2022: 16.1 million). Its name comes from the Sotho-Tswana word for gold, and it was formed in 1994 from part of the old Transvaal, initially as PWV until its renaming in 1995. Gauteng is the wealthiest province and generates about 34% of national [[Gross domestic product|gross domestic product]]. [[Johannesburg]], the provincial capital and largest city, is the financial hub, and [[Pretoria]] is South Africa's administrative capital. Politically, it is the most closely contested province between the [[African National Congress]] and the liberal Democratic Alliance.

Bosnian Serb student and member of Young Bosnia, who assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir presumptive to the throne of [[Austria-Hungary]], and his wife Sophie in [[Sarajevo]] on 28 June 1914. The assassination set off the July Crisis, which led within a month to the outbreak of [[World War I]]. Princip was spared the death penalty because of his age and sentenced to twenty years in prison. He died of [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]], worsened by harsh prison conditions. His legacy is contested: many Serbs regard him as a hero who opposed colonial oppression, while Bosniaks and Croats frequently view him as a [[Terrorism|terrorist]].

Male [[Homosexuality|homosexuals]]. The word *gay* is recommended by LGBTQ groups and style guides for people exclusively attracted to members of the same sex. Gay men continue to face significant discrimination, particularly in parts of Asia and Africa, and in Western countries in daily life, though some, including [[Tim Cook]], have reached prominence. Ancient Egypt has the earliest possible male couple, Khnumhotep and Niankhkhnum, around 2400 BC. In cultures influenced by [[Abrahamic religions]], sodomy was treated as a crime, and most Christian theologians and denominations have considered homosexual behavior sinful. Some scholars, including [[Michel Foucault]], see such terms applied to [[Socrates]] as risking anachronism.
